prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, which brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I put IceCube first in my opening ballot and I still think it is a fine candidate, but reading the full set of ballots has moved me to optical lattice clocks as the candidate to carry forward. Every one of the eight of us ranked B015, five of us in the top three, and two of us first. That is not proof of merit, but it matters that it holds across atomic physicists, a condensed-matter theorist and an astroparticle experimentalist, and that nobody gave a serious scientific objection. On the merits it is what I value in an experimentalist's prize: a clear idea (Katori's magic-wavelength trap, which removes the light shift so that many atoms can be interrogated at once), a decisive demonstration, and a long, patient campaign on systematics that took fractional uncertainty to about 1e-18. The result is reproduced and compared across JILA, RIKEN, NIST, PTB, SYRTE and NPL, and the redefinition of the second is on the table, so the work has already become the reference instrument of its field. It opens tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and dark-matter searches. The two-name attribution (Katori for the concept and first clock, Ye for taking it to record accuracy and exploiting many-body effects) was accepted by all eight openings, which is rare for this list.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution and novelty relative to earlier prizes. Hall and Hansch (2005, frequency combs) and Wineland (2012, control of single trapped ions) cover the enabling tools, and ion-clock leaders and the Paris and PTB groups (for example Lemonde) also pushed the field, so a skeptic can say the clock is the culmination of recognised technology rather than a new discovery. A second worry is timing: the SI second has not yet been redefined, and some colleagues may prefer to wait for that. Finally, I know my own pull toward instrument-building prizes, so I should be careful not to treat precision as the same thing as physical insight. IceCube, in contrast, directly opens a new observational window, and I would not want this committee to drop it because of a credit problem that a better formulation might solve.

responses.point: Ulf ranks IceCube first because the diffuse flux and the TXS 0506+056 association open a new window, with nature giving a clue, and he accepts Halzen and Karle as a coherent pair while noting that AMANDA, DUMAND, Baikal and ANTARES complicate credit.
responses.response: I agree with the physics and my own opening ballot put B014 first for the same reason. Where I have moved is on the readiness of the credit. Eva Olsson and Goran Johansson both question whether two names fairly represent a collaboration of hundreds and the AMANDA lineage, and I cannot dismiss that. Ulf's own ballot says source identification is only individually significant for TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068, so the stable core is the diffuse flux. I would keep B014 as my first alternative rather than the lead, and I would like Ulf to say what he would do about the detector-building credit if a third name had to be dropped.

responses.point: Eva ranks topological insulators first (Kane, Molenkamp, Xue) as a clear theory plus two decisive experiments, but she also puts IceCube fourth with a genuine concern that two individuals may not fairly represent a large collaboration and its original idea.
responses.response: I share her IceCube concern, and it is part of why I am not leading with B014. On B003 I have to be honest that I am relying on colleagues. I ranked it third with only Kane and Molenkamp, because I could not judge how Xue's quantum anomalous Hall experiment belongs in the same prize as the quantum spin Hall effect. Eva and Olle have the expertise, so I would ask whether the QSH and QAH parts are one achievement or two. If they are two, a three-name B003 is easier to cite than the narrow version I proposed, and I would want it explicitly debated against B018, which includes Mele and Hasan.

responses.point: Stefan ranks lattice clocks first as the most precise instruments ever built, with clear linewidth and systematics budgets, independent confirmation, and a clean two-laureate configuration, while noting that Lemonde, Takamoto and the Hall and Hansch comb work are adjacent credits.
responses.response: This is closest to my own reading and it is why I am moving my vote to B015. I would qualify one thing: the adjacent-credit argument deserves a real answer in the citation. I would word it around the optical lattice clock itself and not around clock precision in general, so that it does not read as a second prize for combs or ion control. Stefan's point on the redefinition of the second supports timeliness, but I would not make the prize depend on a metrology-body decision.

responses.point: Goran ranks circuit QED first as the architecture beneath superconducting processors, with theory and experiment tightly linked, but he acknowledges that the 2025 prize on macroscopic tunnelling in circuits already recognised part of this platform.
responses.response: I take his foundational argument seriously, and four of us have B039 in the top four. My difficulty is the 2025 overlap, which he raises himself: Clarke, Devoret and Martinis were honoured in the same circuit-quantum-device territory, and Girvin and Huang are missing from the credited trio. Awarding a second superconducting-circuit prize in consecutive years would be hard to defend when B015 offers a clean, unrecognised achievement. I would rank B039 behind B015, B014 and B003, though I would be glad to hear a better argument that circuit QED is distinct enough.

responses.point: Bernhard alone ranks fluctuation theorems first, as exact, general and experimentally confirmed relations that extend the second law to small and driven systems, while admitting the credit problem with Gallavotti and Cohen.
responses.response: The result is elegant and reproduced, and I do not wish to dismiss it because only one member ranked it first. But I cannot evaluate the Gallavotti-Cohen versus Evans-Searles versus Jarzynski-Crooks priority question, and he himself says it is a real competitor to the credited trio. Until that attribution can be sorted out, I cannot support B005 as a prize configuration, and I would ask him whether he would accept Jarzynski and Crooks alone.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the optical lattice clock as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 frequency comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and whether a citation can keep the credit narrow.
Whether the pending redefinition of the SI second makes this the right year or an argument to wait.
How to split the credit for the IceCube result between Halzen, Karle, AMANDA predecessors and the large collaboration, if B014 comes back as the lead.
Whether B003 should be one or two achievements (quantum spin Hall plus 3D topological insulators versus quantum anomalous Hall), which I cannot judge as a non-specialist.
How much weight to give the 2025 prize when judging B039 and B009.
statement.conflict_note: I am in the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations, which puts me in the same broad astroparticle community as B014 (IceCube) and, to a lesser extent, B045 (pulsar timing). I have no apparent personal or institutional connection to any credited person from my profile, but I would flag the field proximity if B014 is chosen as the lead. No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B015, B003 or the other shortlisted candidates.
